name: Chungthang
tagline: Where two rivers become the Teesta, and where the 2023 flood struck
meta_description: Chungthang: the Lachen–Lachung confluence that forms the Teesta, the Guru Rinpoche rock, the 2023 flood and Teesta III dam, and the road fork today.
summary: Chungthang is the river town at about 1,790 m where the Lachen Chu and Lachung Chu meet to form the Teesta, 95 km from Gangtok and the fork for Lachen and Lachung. The October 2023 flood destroyed the Teesta III dam here and much of the town's riverside. Tours pass through; check current status before you travel.

local_story.title: A blessed valley, a dam and the night of 4 October
paras: Chungthang has long been treated as a holy place. Local Buddhist lore says Guru Padmasambhava rested here on his travels. A rock in the town is said to bear his hand and footprints, with water flowing from a crack in it, and a small patch of ground nearby is said to grow paddy every year from grain he scattered, though rice does not otherwise grow at this height. Some local tellings even link Chungthang to Demazong, the hidden valley of rice, an old name for Sikkim. We pass these on as folklore. The town also has a gurdwara and a large army base.

In 2017 the 1,200 MW Teesta III hydropower project was commissioned at Chungthang. On the night of 3–4 October 2023, after extreme rain, South Lhonak lake in the far north-west burst its moraine wall. The flood reached Chungthang around midnight. Operators tried to open the dam gates after a warning from the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, but the water destroyed the dam within minutes and swept down the Teesta, damaging Chungthang, Dikchu, Singtam and Rangpo and cutting North Sikkim off for months.

did_you_know: Chungthang is 95 km from Gangtok and 28 km from Mangan; it is the fork where the roads to Lachen and Lachung divide.
The South Lhonak lake that burst in 2023 had grown from about 17 hectares in 1977 to about 167 hectares by September 2023.
Downstream of Chungthang, the 2023 flood raised Teesta water levels by 15–20 feet and washed away about fifteen bridges across Sikkim.
intro: For most travellers Chungthang is a checkpoint, a tea stop and a fork in the road. Lachen lies up the left valley, Lachung up the right. Stand on the bridge and you see the two rivers meet: the Lachen Chu from the north-west and the Lachung Chu from the north-east, joining to form the Teesta that flows all the way to Bangladesh.

Since October 2023, Chungthang is also where you see the flood's force most clearly: a wide, raw riverbed of boulders and silt, damaged buildings, rebuilt bridges and the remains of the dam. Road works and diversions here decide whether North Sikkim tours run at all. Spend 20 minutes, buy tea, look and listen. Check current status before you travel.
facts: Teesta confluence, Guru Rinpoche rock, 2023 flood

highlights.title: The confluence
highlights.text: From the bridge area you see the Lachen Chu and Lachung Chu meet and become the Teesta. After 2023 the riverbed is broad and stony. Ask your driver to stop for five minutes; it is the turning point of every North Sikkim trip.

highlights.title: Guru Rinpoche's rock
highlights.text: A rock said to carry the hand and footprints of Guru Padmasambhava, with water flowing from a crack and a patch of paddy nearby. Lore, but loved locally; ask in town for directions.

highlights.title: Seeing the flood's path
highlights.text: The scars of October 2023 are still visible: a widened river, damaged structures and the ruined Teesta III dam. Look respectfully; people here lost homes and family.

highlights.title: The road fork
highlights.text: Left for Lachen and Gurudongmar, right for Lachung and Yumthang. The checkpost here sees every permit, so keep your ID copy handy.

highlights.title: A tea stop with a view
highlights.text: Small hotels and stalls serve tea, momos and simple meals. On the classic tour you often pass through twice, once each way.

how_to_reach.text: Every Lachen and Lachung tour passes through Chungthang, about 95 km and 4–5 hours from Gangtok. Stops are short, for tea, toilets and the permit check.

Shared jeeps run between Gangtok, Mangan and Chungthang for residents. Visitors heading beyond to Lachen or Lachung still need a permit tour; check with the Mangan administration before travelling independently this far.

where_to_stay: Few travellers stay in Chungthang, and after the 2023 flood the options are limited. It is a pass-through town, roughly 1–1.5 hours below both Lachung and Lachen, which have far more rooms. If a road closure stops your vehicle here, drivers know the small hotels in town; expect basic rooms at about ₹1,000–2,000. Otherwise plan nights in Lachung, Lachen, Singhik or Mangan.
tips: Keep your permit and photo ID copies handy for the Chungthang checkpost.
Be careful with photographs: no army installations, and ask before photographing people near damaged homes.
Use the toilet stop here; the next ones are in Lachen or Lachung.
Ask the driver about road conditions ahead; Chungthang is where closures are announced.
If you visit the Guru Rinpoche rock, leave shoes and voices at the gate.

experiences.title: Where the Lachen and Lachung become the Teesta
experiences.summary: At Chungthang the Lachen Chu and the Lachung Chu meet to form the Teesta, the river that runs past Mangan, Gangtok's valley and Siliguri to Bangladesh. Stop near the bridges, find the two streams and see how the 2023 flood reshaped the riverbed.
body: The Teesta is the river of Sikkim. It rises from glacial lakes such as Tso Lhamo on the northern plateau, and its two main upper branches come down the Lachen and Lachung valleys. At Chungthang they meet. From here the Teesta flows south past Mangan, Dikchu, Singtam and Rangpo, through the Darjeeling hills and Siliguri, and on into Bangladesh.

Before 2023 the confluence was a narrow meeting of two rushing streams. The October 2023 flood came down the Lachen Chu side and changed everything: the bed is now broad, grey and full of boulders and silt, with new channels and embankments. You can still see the two waters join, often slightly different in colour.

Ask your driver to stop near the bridge for five to ten minutes. Stand well back from the edge; banks here can be unstable. Avoid photographing army posts and the dam site's security areas. It is a short stop, but it explains the whole valley you have been driving up.

faqs.q: Where does the Teesta River start?
faqs.a: The Teesta begins from glacial lakes and streams on the high plateau of North Sikkim, including Tso Lhamo, fed partly by streams from near Gurudongmar. Its two upper branches, the Lachen Chu and Lachung Chu, meet at Chungthang, which is usually called the start of the Teesta proper.

faqs.q: Can I stop at Chungthang on a North Sikkim tour?
faqs.a: Yes. Most tours stop at Chungthang for tea, toilets and the permit check, often for 15–30 minutes. Ask the driver to stop near the confluence for a few minutes. On the classic loop you pass through twice, so there is usually a chance.

faqs.q: Is it safe to go near the river at Chungthang?
faqs.a: Stay well back. After the 2023 flood the banks are loose in places, and water levels can rise quickly after rain upstream. Watch from the road or bridge, not the water's edge, and keep children close.

experiences.title: Guru Rinpoche's rock and the paddy patch
experiences.summary: Local Buddhist lore says Guru Padmasambhava rested at Chungthang and left hand and footprints on a rock from which water still flows, and that a patch of paddy nearby grows each year from grain he scattered. Ask locally for the shrine and visit quietly.
body: Guru Padmasambhava, Guru Rinpoche, is Sikkim's patron saint, and many places in the state are linked to his travels. Chungthang's story is one of the best known. The lore says he stopped here, and that a rock in the town carries the marks of his hands and feet. From a small opening in the rock, water flows that people collect as blessed.

Nearby, the story goes, is a small patch of ground where he scattered a handful of grain, and where paddy has grown every year since, although rice is not a crop of this altitude. Some local tellings connect Chungthang with Demazong, the hidden valley of rice, an old Tibetan name for Sikkim. These are traditions, and we share them as such.

Ask in town or your driver for the shrine; it is a short walk or drive. Remove shoes where asked, walk clockwise, and do not climb on the rock. A small donation is welcome. Chungthang also has a gurdwara; respect both places and the people who keep them.

faqs.q: What is the Guru Rinpoche rock at Chungthang?
faqs.a: It is a rock that local Buddhist tradition says bears the hand and footprints of Guru Padmasambhava, Sikkim's patron saint, with water flowing from a small opening. Pilgrims visit it and collect the water. It is a matter of faith and folklore rather than history.

faqs.q: Does paddy really grow at Chungthang?
faqs.a: Local lore says a small patch of paddy grows every year near the rock, from grain scattered by Guru Padmasambhava, although rice is not normally grown at this height. Visitors and locals point it out as a blessing. We pass it on as tradition.

faqs.q: Is there a gurdwara at Chungthang?
faqs.a: Yes, Chungthang has a gurdwara as well as Buddhist shrines, and the town has a large army presence. Visitors of all faiths are generally welcome at both if they follow the customs: cover your head at the gurdwara, remove shoes, and keep quiet.

experiences.title: Understanding the 2023 Teesta flood
experiences.summary: On the night of 3–4 October 2023, a glacial lake burst far upstream and the flood destroyed the Teesta III dam at Chungthang within minutes. Stop, look at the riverbed and the rebuilt road, and understand why North Sikkim's roads still close so often.
body: South Lhonak is a glacial lake in Sikkim's far north-west, dammed by a wall of moraine left by a retreating glacier. Scientists had watched it grow for decades, from about 17 hectares in 1977 to around 167 hectares by late September 2023. In 2018 pipes were even carried up by yak to try to pump water out. An early warning system was being installed.

In early October 2023, extreme rain fell over Sikkim. On the night of 3–4 October the lake breached. The flood reached Chungthang around midnight. Dam operators, warned by the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, tried to open the gates, but the 1,200 MW Teesta III dam was destroyed in minutes. Downstream, water rose 15–20 feet and bridges and highway stretches were swept away.

Today you see a widened, grey riverbed, rebuilt sections of road and the remains of the dam. Many local people lost relatives, homes and livelihoods. Ask questions gently, if at all. The flood is the main reason we tell you, again and again, to check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What caused the 2023 Sikkim flood?
faqs.a: Heavy rain in early October 2023 led to the breach of South Lhonak, a glacial lake dammed by moraine in Sikkim's far north-west. The released water became a glacial lake outburst flood down the Teesta, destroying the Teesta III dam at Chungthang and damaging towns and highways downstream.

faqs.q: Is the Teesta III dam still damaged?
faqs.a: The dam was destroyed in the October 2023 flood, along with the bridge to its powerhouse. Repair and rebuilding plans have been discussed since. Visitors see the damaged site from the road; do not enter work or security areas or photograph installations.

faqs.q: Is it safe to travel through Chungthang now?
faqs.a: When the road is open and permits are issued, tours travel through daily. The risk comes from landslides and road damage, especially in the monsoon. Follow the advice of your driver and the authorities, avoid monsoon travel, and check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: A rice-and-dal lunch at the fork
experiences.image_query: Sikkim roadside hotel dal bhat lunch
experiences.summary: Many North Sikkim tours stop for lunch around Chungthang. Small hotels serve rice, dal, a vegetable, pickle and sometimes chicken or eggs for about ₹150–250. It is plain, filling food, and one of the best-value meals of the trip.
body: On the long drive between Gangtok and Lachen or Lachung, lunch often lands at Chungthang or just before it. The small hotels by the road serve the standard Sikkim highway meal: steamed rice, dal, a seasonal vegetable such as squash, potato or local greens, a pickle, and sometimes eggs or chicken curry.

A plate costs about ₹150–250, with refills of rice and dal usually free. Momos and thukpa are around ₹100–180. Tea is ₹20–40. Ask for local greens if they have them; fern shoots, called ningro, and squash shoots appear in season.

Eat simply here, especially if you are heading for Lachen and a 3 am start for Gurudongmar. Avoid very spicy or oily food before the hairpins. Carry bottled or filtered water, and use the toilet before leaving. Pay in cash; network and card machines are unreliable after the flood.

faqs.q: Where do North Sikkim tours stop for lunch?
faqs.a: Commonly at Mangan, Singhik or Chungthang, depending on the start time, traffic and road works. Small hotels serve rice, dal, vegetables and meat for ₹150–250. Lunch is usually not included in shared packages, so carry cash.

faqs.q: Is vegetarian food available at Chungthang?
faqs.a: Yes. The standard lunch of rice, dal, vegetable and pickle is vegetarian, and momos and thukpa come in vegetable versions. Strict Jain diets are harder; carry some dry snacks if you need them.

faqs.q: Is lunch included in the North Sikkim tour?
faqs.a: Usually not on the travel days. Shared packages generally include dinner and breakfast at Lachen and Lachung, but lunches on the road are paid separately, about ₹150–250 per person. Check what your package covers when you book.

faqs.q: Where is Chungthang?
faqs.a: Chungthang is in North Sikkim, about 95 km north of Gangtok and 28 km beyond Mangan, at roughly 1,790 m. It sits where the Lachen Chu and Lachung Chu meet to form the Teesta River, and the roads to Lachen and Lachung divide here.

faqs.q: What happened at Chungthang in 2023?
faqs.a: On the night of 3–4 October 2023, a flood from the burst South Lhonak glacial lake reached Chungthang around midnight and destroyed the 1,200 MW Teesta III dam within minutes. The town's riverside, roads and bridges were badly damaged, and North Sikkim was cut off for a long period.

faqs.q: Is Chungthang open for tourists?
faqs.a: Tours pass through Chungthang whenever the North Sikkim road and permits are open. Closures since 2023 have often been decided by road conditions around Chungthang and on the Lachen side. Check current status before you travel with your agent and the district administration.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Chungthang?
faqs.a: Chungthang has a checkpost where North Sikkim permits are checked, and travellers going on to Lachen or Lachung need the permit arranged by a registered Gangtok operator. If you want to visit Chungthang itself independently, ask the Mangan district administration about current rules.

faqs.q: Is there anywhere to stay in Chungthang?
faqs.a: There are a few small hotels, mainly used by officials, drivers and travellers held up by road closures. Rooms are basic, about ₹1,000–2,000. Most travellers stay in Lachung, Lachen, Singhik or Mangan instead, where there are more and better options.

faqs.q: What is the Guru Padmasambhava rock in Chungthang?
faqs.a: A rock that local Buddhist tradition says carries the hand and footprints of Guru Padmasambhava, with water flowing from it and a patch of paddy growing nearby from grain he scattered. Pilgrims visit and collect the water. It is folklore and faith, not documented history.

faqs.q: How long is the drive from Chungthang to Lachung?
faqs.a: About 22 km and 1–1.5 hours to Lachung, depending on road works. Lachen is about 28 km, around 1.5 hours. Since 2023 both roads have had rebuilt sections, diversions and closures. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why is there an army base at Chungthang?
faqs.a: Chungthang is the gateway to the border valleys of Lachen and Lachung, which lead toward the Tibetan plateau, so the Indian Army keeps a major forward base and medical centre here. Do not photograph military installations, vehicles or personnel anywhere in the area.

faqs.q: Can I see the Teesta III dam?
faqs.a: You can see parts of the damaged dam site from the road. Do not enter construction or security areas, and do not photograph them if signs or guards say no. The site is a reminder of the 2023 flood, so treat it with respect.
